title: Catching up with AI
text:
Why this site exists
For the last 15 years, I have worked in bioinformatics and biomedical data science, developing data analysis pipelines and supporting scientific research. During that time, artificial intelligence evolved rapidly — particularly in areas such as deep learning and, more recently, generative AI.
Like many scientists working with data, I realised at some point that I had developed a knowledge gap. I was comfortable with statistical modelling, genomic data analysis and scientific computing, but the knowledge around large language models (LLMs) and AI-assisted workflows had largely evolved outside my day-to-day work.
This notebook is my way of catching up. It collects my notes along the way — part learning log, part technical guide. I try to document not just what I learn, but also how I learn it, what I find confusing and what actually turns out to be useful in practice.

title: Catching up with AI
text:
How I started
I started exploring generative AI with tools such as ChatGPT and Perplexity, followed tutorials from the OpenAI Academy and took online courses on prompt engineering, custom AI assistants and AI-assisted data analysis.
But I wanted to understand more than just how to use these tools. How do they actually work? How reliable are they? And how might they be integrated into computational and scientific workflows? This also made me realise that I needed a more systematic understanding of machine learning and neural networks. Over the years, I had picked up bits and pieces, but never really developed a solid foundation in either.
At the same time, I wanted to learn how to work with AI coding assistants, as this is clearly becoming an increasingly relevant skill in software development. I was also particularly interested in understanding what AI could actually contribute to scientific research.
AI is often presented as something that will fundamentally change how we work and do research. Undoubtedly, it is a powerful technology, but generative AI is still relatively young. Many of the tools, methods and skills for working with it are still being developed, and the field itself is still taking shape. At the same time, the limitations and risks of AI — from unreliable outputs and bias to questions around privacy, accountability and responsible use — are becoming increasingly important to understand. It is therefore not always easy to distinguish genuine progress from the surrounding hype.

title: Catching up with AI
text:
How this notebook is organised
The material is organised into five broad areas:

Foundations — Learning the foundations of machine learning and neural networks, and understanding the concepts behind modern generative AI.
Working with AI — Exploring prompt engineering, human–AI workflows, data analysis and the critical use of AI assistants.
Building with AI — Learning how AI can become part of computational work, from configured assistants and AI-assisted coding to grounding models with data and building AI-enabled workflows.
AI for Science — Exploring how AI can support literature discovery, scientific reasoning, data analysis and communication, and where it may become useful as a research tool.
Responsible AI — Examining the limitations, risks, ethical considerations and legal frameworks surrounding AI, particularly in scientific research.

This notebook is not intended as a comprehensive guide to artificial intelligence. The chapters simply reflect the topics I am interested in and want to learn more about.

title: Catching up with AI
text:
Notes, reflections and updates
AI is developing quickly, and my own understanding is (hopefully) evolving with it. Rather than continually rewriting earlier material, I want to preserve the context in which I learned something and add new observations or corrections as my understanding changes.
In addition to the main chapters, I have included two sections for notes and updates:

Notes, Reflections & Updates — Personal observations, experiments, open questions and changes in my understanding.
AI Developments & Updates — Selected developments in AI technology, scientific applications and regulation that are relevant to the subjects explored here.

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Prompt engineering
These notes are based on the Coursera courses Prompt Engineering for ChatGPT and Advanced Prompt Engineering for Everyone by Jules White at Vanderbilt University. These courses were how I first learned to work systematically with large language models. The material I present here has subsequently been organized and adapted from my original course notes.
Prompt patterns are reusable strategies for interacting with large language models — or, as I would call it, “the art of talking to the machine.” For users and developers learning to work with LLMs, prompt patterns provide a systematic way of thinking about how to formulate instructions, guide the interaction and shape the resulting output. The idea follows the concept of design patterns in software engineering, where a general solution can be adapted to different problems and contexts (White et al. 2023).
Although prompt patterns provide a systematic approach, interacting with a language model is not a rigid process. Different users develop their own ways of working with AI, depending on their background, tasks and preferences. What works well for one person or task may not necessarily work for another.
A prompt is the input given to a large language model. It can contain a question or task, but also additional context, constraints, examples, or instructions about the expected output.
Prompt engineering is the process of designing this input to guide the model towards a useful response. Some of the basic elements that can be specified in a prompt include:
For example, instead of simply asking:
the task can be made more specific:
Similarly, instead of:
a more specific prompt might be:
The additional information communicates not only the topic, but also the expected level, focus and form of the response.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Persona pattern
The Persona Pattern asks the model to adopt a particular role or perspective. This can influence the terminology, level of expertise and type of response.

Act as a senior bioinformatician experienced in single-cell epigenomics. Provide actionable suggestions.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Audience Persona pattern
The Audience Persona Pattern specifies who the response is intended for so that the explanation can be adapted to their background.

Assume I am new to machine learning but familiar with R and statistics. Explain what a transformer is.

The distinction is useful: the Persona Pattern describes the perspective from which the model should respond, whereas the Audience Persona Pattern describes the person for whom the response is intended.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Question Refinement pattern
Sometimes the original question itself has been poorly specified. The Question Refinement Pattern asks the model to improve or clarify the question before answering it.

When I ask you something unclear, suggest a more precise version first and ask whether I want to use it.

This can be useful for technical problems where small differences in the formulation of the question can change what is actually being asked.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Flipped Interaction pattern
Normally, the user asks questions and the model answers them. The Flipped Interaction Pattern reverses this relationship: the model asks the user questions until it has enough information to perform the task.

Ask me clarifying questions until you can design a workshop outline. When you have enough information, present the final outline.

This is useful when the information required to complete a task is not known in advance or would be cumbersome to specify in a single prompt.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Few-shot prompting
With few-shot prompting, examples of the desired input-output relationship are included directly in the prompt. The model can then infer the pattern from those examples.
For example:

Input: ATGCGT Output: reversed sequence: TGCGTA
Input: AACCAT Output:

Examples can be particularly useful for classification, extraction, transformation, or formatting tasks.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Chain-of-Thought prompting
Chain-of-Thought prompting encourages the model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before producing an answer.
Something like:

Show your reasoning in short bullet points and end with a final answer.

The idea is to break the problem down into smaller steps instead of asking the model to produce the final answer straight away.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
ReAct
ReAct is an approach that combines reasoning with actions performed using external tools. Instead of producing an answer only from the prompt and its internal context, the model can alternate between deciding what to do, performing an action, and using the result to continue the task.
Conceptually:
reason → act → inspect → continue → answer
For example, with access to appropriate tools:

Search PubMed for recent papers on DNA methylation in HSCs, summarize the main findings, and explain how they relate to AML biology.

This introduces the important idea that interactions with language models can extend beyond prompting itself: models can be connected to tools and external information sources.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Alternative Approaches pattern
Rather than asking for one solution, the Alternative Approaches Pattern asks the model to explore several possible strategies.

Propose five different ways to create a metadata-capture workflow for a small lab, ranked by feasibility.

This can be useful for brainstorming, planning and problems where there is no single obvious solution.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Evaluation pattern
The Evaluation Pattern provides explicit criteria against which an output should be assessed.

Here are three example abstracts. Score the following abstract for clarity (1–5), structure (1–5), and scientific accuracy (1–5). Provide a justification for each score.

Explicit criteria make the basis of the evaluation clearer and can make different outputs easier to compare.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Game Play pattern
The Game Play Pattern introduces rules that turn an interaction into a structured exercise.

We are going to play a game. I describe a laboratory workflow. You identify five mistakes a junior researcher might make and suggest how each could be avoided.

The rules constrain the interaction while still allowing the content to change between rounds.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Recipe pattern
The Recipe Pattern is useful when part of a sequence or procedure is already known and the model is asked to complete or refine it.
For example:

Complete the missing steps in this workflow:

Load FASTQ files
[…]
Align reads using BWA
[…]
Generate a BAM summary


This allows existing knowledge or constraints to be incorporated rather than asking the model to generate an entire workflow from scratch.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Template pattern
The Template Pattern specifies the structure in which information should be returned.
For example:

Mutation Summary Gene: <GENE> Variant: <VARIANT> Impact: <IMPACT> Evidence: <QUOTES FROM ARTICLE>

Templates are useful when similar information needs to be extracted or presented consistently across multiple inputs.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Semantic Filter
A Semantic Filter specifies information that should be removed or transformed while preserving the remainder.

Remove all dates from the text but change as little as possible.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Meta-language pattern
The Meta-language Pattern defines a shorthand or small domain-specific vocabulary that has a particular meaning within the interaction.

When I write QC-S1, interpret it as: run initial QC on sequencing files and summarize FastQC results.

This allows frequently used instructions to be represented using a more compact notation.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Tail Generation
Tail Generation automatically adds a specified operation or output after the main task has been completed.

After summarizing the paper, append a list of unresolved questions.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Cognitive Verifier pattern
The Cognitive Verifier Pattern breaks a larger question into additional questions whose answers can be used to construct the final response (White et al. 2023).
Rather than answering the original question immediately, the model first identifies additional questions that need to be answered. The answers to these questions are then combined to produce the final response.
Unlike Chain-of-Thought, which focuses on the reasoning steps used to solve a problem, the Cognitive Verifier Pattern focuses on which additional questions need to be answered before the original question can be answered well.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns
text:
Fact Check List pattern
The Fact Check List Pattern asks the model to identify factual statements in its output that should be checked.
For example:

Extract the factual claims from the response and list those that require verification.

Importantly, identifying claims that require verification is not the same as independently verifying them. The claims still need to be checked against appropriate sources.
crumbs: 2  2.1 Prompt engineering and prompt patterns

title: 2.2 Working with data, documents and files
text:
These notes are based on the Coursera course Advanced Data Analysis with ChatGPT by Jules White at Vanderbilt University. After learning how to formulate prompts and use prompt patterns, the next step is learning how to bring information into the interaction and work with it.
Working with datasets, documents and other files shifts the focus from how to formulate a prompt to what information the model has available and how it is presented.
Files can provide both the material to work with and information that the model needs to complete a task. This might involve analysing datasets, extracting information from documents, comparing sources or transforming files. A useful first step is to inspect the material rather than immediately requesting a final result.

Working with data
When working with a data file, it is useful to understand its structure before starting the analysis.
A simple workflow might be:
load → inspect → clean and transform → analyse → visualise → interpret
For example, imagine uploading a table containing gene-expression measurements for a set of samples.
First, inspect the data:

Inspect this dataset. Report its dimensions, column names and data types, identify missing values, and provide basic summary statistics. Do not perform any further analysis yet.

Next, examine whether the data need cleaning or transformation:

Check whether the expression values require transformation and whether there are obvious problems with the data. Explain what you find before making any changes.

Then, perform the analysis:

Compare the two experimental groups and identify genes showing the largest differences in expression. Create an appropriate visualisation of the results.

Finally, interpret the results:

Explain what the visualisation shows and identify any patterns or observations that should be investigated further.

In this way, intermediate results can be inspected before deciding what to do next.
Importantly, the language model does not necessarily perform all these operations itself. Depending on the environment, it can use computational tools such as Python to manipulate data, perform calculations and create visualisations. The model can help formulate the analysis, generate or execute code, and interpret the resulting output.


Working with documents
Documents can be used in different ways depending on the task. A useful distinction is between treating a document as an object and treating a document as knowledge.
When working with a document as an object, the task concerns the document itself, such as extracting text, reorganising sections or changing its format.

Extract the tables from this document and return them in a structured format.

When working with a document as knowledge, its content provides information needed to answer a question or perform another task.

Read this paper and summarise the main findings, methods and limitations.

Several documents can also be brought together:

Compare the conclusions of these three papers. Identify where they agree, where they differ, and which evidence each paper provides for its conclusions.



Bringing information into the conversation
When working with larger documents or several sources, it can be useful to extract relevant information and bring it into the conversation in a more manageable form.
Also, the amount of information that can be provided to a language model at once is limited by its context window. Long documents or collections of documents may therefore need to be summarised or divided into smaller pieces. This can also help keep the interaction focused on information relevant to the task.
For example:

Extract the information relevant to this question and present it in a form that I can quickly verify.

For larger collections, an index or structured overview can help organise the information while retaining its source:

Create a table listing the relevant information, the document it came from, and where in the document it was found.

For example:



Information
Source
Location




Finding or statement
Document A
Page 4


Finding or statement
Document B
Results section


Finding or statement
Document C
Table 2



Keeping information connected to its original source makes it easier to inspect, verify and return to the source when necessary. This is particularly important when information is summarised or combined across several documents.

title: 2.3 Human–AI workflows
text:
These notes are also based on the Coursera course Advanced Data Analysis with ChatGPT by Jules White at Vanderbilt University. While the previous section focused on working with data, documents and files, this section takes a broader view of how more complex tasks can be organised as workflows involving humans, AI and other computational tools.
Working with a language model becomes more complicated when a task involves several steps. Rather than describing the entire task in a single prompt, it can be useful to think in terms of a workflow: how the task can be divided into steps, what each step requires and produces, and which parts should be performed by humans, AI or other computational tools.

From prompts to workflows
A larger task can usually be divided into a sequence of smaller steps, where the output of one step becomes the input for another.
For example, analysing a collection of scientific papers might involve:
identify relevant papers → extract information → organise the information → compare findings → interpret differences → produce a summary
Not all of these steps necessarily require the same approach. Some may involve a language model, others may require search or computational tools, and some depend on human judgement.


ETAC: structuring a larger task
One framework suggested by Jules White for breaking down larger tasks is ETAC:
Extract → Transform → Analyze → Create
The four stages describe different operations that may occur within a workflow. For example, when working with a collection of scientific papers:








Stage
Purpose
Scientific-paper example




Extract
Retrieve relevant information
Identify findings and retain their sources


Transform
Organise, clean or convert information
Structure findings for comparison


Analyze
Examine patterns and relationships
Compare findings and supporting evidence


Create
Produce an output
Prepare a summary or report



ETAC provides a simple way of thinking about the different stages of a task. In practice, however, a workflow does not always proceed neatly from Extract to Transform to Analyze to Create. Individual steps may need to be repeated, intermediate results inspected, and earlier decisions revised before moving on.


Dividing work between humans, AI and tools
Breaking a task into steps also makes it possible to consider who or what should perform each step. A workflow can combine human judgement, language models and other computational tools.
Different parts of a task are suited to different approaches. A language model can help extract and organise information, generate alternatives, explain results or plan the next step. Python or other computational tools can perform calculations, manipulate data and create visualisations, while specialised software may be needed for domain-specific analyses.
The human remains responsible for directing the workflow: defining the objective, providing relevant context, deciding which approaches are appropriate, inspecting intermediate results and judging whether the final result makes sense.
For example, in a data-analysis workflow, the work might be divided like this:



Step
Possible role




Define the scientific question
Human


Inspect the structure of the dataset
AI + computational tools


Decide on an appropriate analysis
Human + AI


Perform calculations
Computational tools


Inspect and visualise results
Human + AI + computational tools


Interpret the results
Human + AI


Evaluate whether the conclusions are justified
Human



These roles are not fixed. They depend on the task, available tools and consequences of an error. The important question is not whether a task should be performed by AI or a human, but how their capabilities can be combined effectively.


Working iteratively
Larger tasks do not necessarily need to be planned completely before starting. A useful approach is to work iteratively:
plan → execute → inspect → adjust → continue



An iterative human–AI workflow: plan, execute, inspect and adjust, then continue with the next step.


A first plan provides a starting point, but each step can produce new information that changes what should happen next. Intermediate results can be inspected before continuing, and the workflow adjusted when something unexpected appears.
For example, a data-analysis task might begin with a plan to inspect the data, clean it, perform an analysis and visualise the results. Inspecting the data may reveal missing values, unexpected distributions or problems with the experimental groups. These observations can change the next step rather than simply continuing with the original plan.
Working in smaller steps also makes it easier to identify where something has gone wrong. If the final result is unexpected, intermediate outputs provide points at which the workflow can be examined and revised.


Assembling larger tasks
Breaking a larger task into smaller pieces makes the individual steps easier to manage, but the results eventually need to be brought together again.
For example, preparing a report from several sources might involve extracting information, organising tables, performing analyses and drafting individual sections. These intermediate outputs can be saved as files or structured data and then assembled into the final report.

title: 2.4 Verification and critical use
text:
These notes are based on the Coursera course Trustworthy Generative AI by Jules White at Vanderbilt University. The previous sections focused on how to interact with AI, work with different types of information and organise more complex tasks as workflows. This section adds another important part of working with generative AI: verifying its outputs and using them critically.
Language models generate text, not necessarily answers. Some of that text may provide useful answers, but even a clear and convincing response can be wrong. This makes verification an important part of working with generative AI.

Why verification matters
Language models generate responses based on patterns learned from data. They can produce incorrect information, make unsupported claims or invent details that appear plausible. These errors are often referred to as hallucinations.
The difficulty is that incorrect answers do not necessarily look incorrect. A response can be fluent and internally coherent while still containing factual errors.
The level of verification should depend on the task and its consequences. A suggestion used for brainstorming does not require the same level of checking as information used in a scientific analysis or an important decision.


When is AI the right tool?
An important part of using AI critically is deciding whether it is appropriate for a particular task in the first place.
Language models can be useful for exploring ideas, working with unstructured information, drafting text, generating code or helping to plan an analysis. However, not every task benefits from involving AI.
For calculations, statistical analyses or data transformations that require precise and reproducible results, conventional computational tools may be more appropriate. AI can still help formulate the approach or generate code, but the actual operations should be performed using methods that can be inspected and tested.
Other considerations include the availability of reliable information, the sensitivity of the data, the consequences of an error and whether the output can be verified.

Before uploading data or documents to an AI service, it is important to consider whether they contain personal, confidential or unpublished information. The service’s data-handling policies and any applicable institutional requirements should be checked before sharing such material.
The question is therefore not simply what AI can do, but whether using AI provides an advantage over existing approaches, given the effort and risks involved.


Checking information and sources
When an answer depends on factual information, an important form of verification is to return to the original source.
Keeping extracted information connected to its source, including document names, page numbers or sections, makes individual statements easier to check.
For example:

Summarise the main findings of these papers. For each finding, identify the supporting paper and section, and provide a short quotation from the original text so that I can verify the interpretation.

References generated by a language model also need to be treated carefully. A citation that looks plausible is not necessarily real, and a real paper does not necessarily support the claim for which it is cited. Both the existence of the source and the connection between the source and the claim need to be checked, including whether any quoted passage accurately reflects the original text.


Checking calculations and analyses
Calculations and data analyses can often be checked independently using conventional computational methods, such as reproducing calculations, inspecting generated code or comparing results with an independent analysis.
Another approach is to test a procedure on a simple case where the expected result is already known.
For example:

Apply this transformation to these five example values and show the result for each value.

The output can then be compared with the expected values before applying the procedure to a larger dataset.
This is particularly important for generated code: code that runs without errors is not necessarily correct. Its behaviour and results still need to be checked against what it was intended to do.


Checking intermediate results
In a multi-step workflow, verification should not be limited to the final result. Important intermediate outputs can be checked before they become inputs to later stages.
Consider a simple workflow:
extract information → organise it → analyse it → produce a summary
If information is extracted incorrectly in the first step, the later analysis may still appear coherent while being based on incorrect input.
Checking intermediate results helps detect errors before they propagate through the workflow and makes it easier to identify where something went wrong.


The cost of verification
AI can produce an answer, analysis or draft very quickly, but generating the output is only part of the work. The result may also need to be checked.
This raises an important question:

How much effort is required to verify the result?

For some tasks, verification is relatively straightforward: a calculation can be reproduced, code can be tested or a statement checked against an identified source. For others, such as evaluating a complex analysis or comparing information across many documents, verification may require substantial work.
The usefulness of AI therefore depends not only on how quickly it produces an output, but also on the cost of establishing whether that output is reliable. Designing workflows with inspectable intermediate results and traceable sources can help reduce that cost.


Domain expertise and human judgement
Some errors can be detected mechanically: a calculation produces the wrong value, a reference does not exist or code fails a test. Other problems are harder to identify. An analysis may use an inappropriate method, an interpretation may overlook an alternative explanation, or a conclusion may go beyond what the evidence supports.
Recognising these problems requires domain expertise and judgement. Someone familiar with the subject may identify implausible assumptions, missing information or methodological problems that are not obvious from the generated answer.
Human expertise therefore remains important throughout the workflow: defining what needs to be checked, evaluating intermediate results and judging whether the evidence supports the conclusions.
Using AI does not transfer responsibility for the resulting work to the model. Anyone incorporating AI-generated information, analyses or text into their work remains responsible for understanding and evaluating what they ultimately use or communicate.

title: 3.1 Configured AI assistants
text:
These notes are based on courses from OpenAI Academy and the Coursera course OpenAI GPTs: Creating your own custom AI assistant by Jules White at Vanderbilt University. After exploring different ways of working with general-purpose AI assistants, I became interested in how they could be configured for more specific tasks and contexts.
General-purpose AI assistants can support a wide range of tasks, but using them repeatedly for a particular purpose often involves providing the same instructions, preferences and contextual information again and again.
Configured AI assistants offer a way to make these interactions more consistent. Rather than starting with a general-purpose assistant each time, we can define its purpose, behaviour and available information in advance.
One approach I explored was Custom GPTs, which allowed users to configure specialised versions of ChatGPT without programming. My interest was not yet in building sophisticated applications, but in starting with a more accessible approach and understanding how far configuration alone could take me and where its limitations became apparent.

What makes an assistant configurable?
A configured assistant typically combines several elements:







Component
Purpose




Instructions
Define the assistant’s role, scope, behaviour and constraints


Context and knowledge
Provide task-specific information, preferences or reference documents


Capabilities and tools
Extend what the assistant can do beyond generating text


Interaction design
Specify what information to request and how to guide the conversation


Output requirements
Define the structure, format and level of detail of responses



These components serve different purposes.
Instructions influence how the assistant behaves, while contextual information and reference documents provide material it can use when responding. Tools may allow the assistant to perform additional operations, such as working with files, analysing data or accessing external information.
Importantly, configuring an assistant does not ordinarily involve retraining the underlying language model. The model remains the same; what changes is the information and instructions provided to it, along with the capabilities made available through the surrounding application.
This distinction is relevant when considering reliability. A configured assistant may behave more consistently within its intended scope, but configuration alone does not guarantee factual accuracy or successful task completion.


Designing instructions and workflows
Configuring an assistant involves more than assigning it a role or defining a preferred tone.
For recurring tasks, it can be useful to specify how the assistant should interact with the user, which information it should collect, what decisions it should make and how the results should be presented.
For example, instructions may require an assistant to:

Ask for missing information before proceeding.
Follow a sequence of steps rather than immediately producing a final answer.
Use particular rules or criteria when generating recommendations.
Produce outputs in a specified format.
Indicate uncertainty instead of inventing missing information.
Request human review or approval before continuing.

These instructions resemble a workflow, but there is an important distinction between describing a workflow in natural language and enforcing it programmatically.
A language model may follow a carefully written sequence of instructions, but its behaviour is not guaranteed. Similarly, instructing an assistant to avoid unsupported claims does not ensure that it will always do so.
The effectiveness of a configuration therefore needs to be assessed through use and testing rather than assumed from the instructions themselves.


Practical experiments with Custom GPTs
I experimented with three Custom GPTs designed to support different recurring tasks. Each had a defined purpose, interaction rules and output requirements.
Although the applications were quite different, they provided useful opportunities to examine how well a language model follows persistent instructions and what happens when those instructions are insufficient.

Experiment 1: Fit & Fun MealBuddy
My first experiment was Fit & Fun MealBuddy, a family meal-planning assistant.
The aim was to simplify everyday meal planning by incorporating information about family members, dietary preferences, physical activities and available cooking time.
The configuration included:

User profiles and dietary preferences.
Questions about planned activities and who would be eating.
Rules for adapting meals to sport and rest days.
Requirements for quick, practical weekday meals.
Output formats for daily plans, weekly plans and grocery lists.
An example conversation illustrating the intended interaction.

The assistant was instructed to ask a series of questions before suggesting meals. It would first establish whether the day involved sporting activities, then identify who would be eating and finally determine the desired output format.
It also included nutritional guidance and rules for adapting meals to different circumstances.
Observations and limitations
Overall, MealBuddy followed its configuration well. It consistently asked the intended questions, accounted for dietary requirements, including vegetarian preferences, and produced outputs in the requested formats.
The initial meal suggestions were generally practical and varied. However, I noticed that new conversations often started with the same or very similar recommendations.
Asking for alternatives revealed another limitation. The first alternative was usually still reasonable, but subsequent suggestions became increasingly impractical. Some combinations of ingredients did not work particularly well together, while others were difficult to prepare.
This was an interesting example of the difference between instruction adherence and recommendation quality. The assistant followed the intended interaction structure, but that did not guarantee diversity, practicality or culinary coherence across repeated requests.
It also showed that testing an assistant with a single successful interaction is insufficient. Some limitations only became apparent through repeated use.


Experiment 2: Note Organizer
My second experiment was Note Organizer, an assistant designed to convert photographs of handwritten notes into structured digital documents.
The motivation was to reduce the effort involved in transcribing and reorganising handwritten material.
The configuration defined three main tasks:

Extract text from photographs of handwritten pages.
Organise and edit the extracted material into coherent sections.
Produce structured text, with Markdown or R Markdown available on request.

The assistant was also instructed to follow a sequential workflow: collect the photographs, ask for contextual information and wait until all pages had been uploaded before processing the notes.
An important part of the configuration concerned preserving the original information. The assistant was instructed not to introduce new concepts, to mark uncertain passages as [unclear] and to add explanatory examples only with explicit permission.
Observations and limitations
The assistant performed surprisingly well at recognising my handwriting. It also generally followed the intended page-by-page workflow.
However, preserving the original content proved more difficult. Despite explicit instructions not to invent information, the assistant occasionally introduced details that were not present in my notes.
The resulting documents also required several rounds of review and restructuring before I was satisfied with them.
Nevertheless, I found the assistant very useful. It substantially reduced the effort involved in creating an initial digital version of handwritten notes, even though the output still required careful editing.
This experiment highlighted the distinction between recognising information and faithfully interpreting it. Accurate transcription does not necessarily imply that the model will preserve the meaning of incomplete or ambiguous notes when reorganising them into coherent text.
It also demonstrated that instructions intended to prevent unsupported additions do not always work as expected.


Experiment 3: Job Application Assistant
My third experiment was a Custom GPT designed to support job applications in bioinformatics, biomedical data science and related research or leadership positions.
Unlike the previous assistants, this one was configured to support a more complex workflow involving document analysis, critical assessment, iterative editing and document generation.
The assistant was intended to work with my existing CV and a specific job advertisement.
Its workflow included:

Analyse the job advertisement and identify its requirements.
Assess how well my experience matched the position, including gaps and potential mismatches.
Save the original job advertisement.
Adapt my CV to the position without inventing or exaggerating qualifications.
Present the revised CV for review and approval.
Prepare a tailored cover letter if requested.
Export the approved documents to Word.

I explicitly instructed the assistant to provide critical rather than overly supportive feedback. It was also asked to distinguish between established expertise and areas in which I was developing my skills, and to avoid generic, overly polished language.
The configuration included several human review and approval stages, with the intention of retaining control over the final application documents.
Observations and limitations
The assistant generally performed well at critically assessing my suitability for different positions. It identified relevant experience and gaps without inventing qualifications or exaggerating my background.
It also respected the intended review stages.
However, the generated CVs and cover letters still required substantial editing. Some formulations were vague or unnecessarily technical, and the writing often had a recognisably AI-generated quality. I needed to revise the text to reflect my own voice and accurately position my experience for each application.
Document generation proved particularly unreliable. Despite explicit instructions to produce complete Word documents and preserve the original formatting, the results were inconsistent. Sometimes documents contained only part of the content, formatting was incorrect, or no Word document was produced.
Eventually, I switched to working with Markdown, which proved considerably more reliable for reviewing and editing the text.
This experiment highlighted several distinctions:

Factual accuracy is not the same as writing quality. An assistant can avoid inventing information while still producing generic or poorly tailored text.
Following a workflow is not the same as completing it successfully. The assistant respected the review stages but struggled with document production.
Content generation and document export are separate capabilities. Producing useful text does not guarantee that a correctly formatted document can be generated.

Overall, the assistant was useful for analysing job requirements and developing initial drafts, but the final applications still depended heavily on human judgement and editing.



What did these experiments teach me?
The three experiments differed considerably in purpose, but they revealed some common strengths and limitations.

The most obvious advantage of configured assistants was that they reduced the need to repeat instructions and made recurring tasks easier to initiate.
They were also generally successful at following structured interaction patterns, including asking questions and waiting for input or approval.
However, their limitations differed depending on the task. MealBuddy struggled to maintain the quality of generated recommendations, Note Organizer sometimes altered the information it was supposed to preserve, and the Job Application Assistant encountered difficulties with writing quality and document production.
These are not necessarily the same kind of failure. Some concern the model’s generated content, while others relate to the tools and functionality of the surrounding application.
One particularly useful lesson was that a successful initial response does not necessarily indicate reliable performance across repeated interactions or more demanding requests.
The experiments also reinforced the importance of keeping a human involved, not simply to approve the final result but to assess whether it is accurate, appropriate and useful.


From configured assistants to AI-enabled systems
Custom GPTs provided an accessible way to experiment with task-specific AI assistants without writing code. They helped me understand the role of instructions, contextual information, interaction design and tools in shaping an assistant’s behaviour.
At the same time, these experiments exposed limitations that cannot necessarily be resolved by writing more detailed instructions.
More reliable systems may require explicit workflow control, better ways of providing and retrieving information, validation of intermediate results, and mechanisms for evaluating performance over time.
These are some of the questions I want to explore next as I move from configuring assistants towards understanding how AI-enabled applications and workflows are built.

title: 3.1 Configured AI assistants
text:
Designing instructions and workflows
Configuring an assistant involves more than assigning it a role or defining a preferred tone.
For recurring tasks, it can be useful to specify how the assistant should interact with the user, which information it should collect, what decisions it should make and how the results should be presented.
For example, instructions may require an assistant to:

Ask for missing information before proceeding.
Follow a sequence of steps rather than immediately producing a final answer.
Use particular rules or criteria when generating recommendations.
Produce outputs in a specified format.
Indicate uncertainty instead of inventing missing information.
Request human review or approval before continuing.

These instructions resemble a workflow, but there is an important distinction between describing a workflow in natural language and enforcing it programmatically.
A language model may follow a carefully written sequence of instructions, but its behaviour is not guaranteed. Similarly, instructing an assistant to avoid unsupported claims does not ensure that it will always do so.
The effectiveness of a configuration therefore needs to be assessed through use and testing rather than assumed from the instructions themselves.

title: 3.1 Configured AI assistants
text:
Practical experiments with Custom GPTs
I experimented with three Custom GPTs designed to support different recurring tasks. Each had a defined purpose, interaction rules and output requirements.
Although the applications were quite different, they provided useful opportunities to examine how well a language model follows persistent instructions and what happens when those instructions are insufficient.

Experiment 1: Fit & Fun MealBuddy
My first experiment was Fit & Fun MealBuddy, a family meal-planning assistant.
The aim was to simplify everyday meal planning by incorporating information about family members, dietary preferences, physical activities and available cooking time.
The configuration included:

User profiles and dietary preferences.
Questions about planned activities and who would be eating.
Rules for adapting meals to sport and rest days.
Requirements for quick, practical weekday meals.
Output formats for daily plans, weekly plans and grocery lists.
An example conversation illustrating the intended interaction.

The assistant was instructed to ask a series of questions before suggesting meals. It would first establish whether the day involved sporting activities, then identify who would be eating and finally determine the desired output format.
It also included nutritional guidance and rules for adapting meals to different circumstances.
Observations and limitations
Overall, MealBuddy followed its configuration well. It consistently asked the intended questions, accounted for dietary requirements, including vegetarian preferences, and produced outputs in the requested formats.
The initial meal suggestions were generally practical and varied. However, I noticed that new conversations often started with the same or very similar recommendations.
Asking for alternatives revealed another limitation. The first alternative was usually still reasonable, but subsequent suggestions became increasingly impractical. Some combinations of ingredients did not work particularly well together, while others were difficult to prepare.
This was an interesting example of the difference between instruction adherence and recommendation quality. The assistant followed the intended interaction structure, but that did not guarantee diversity, practicality or culinary coherence across repeated requests.
It also showed that testing an assistant with a single successful interaction is insufficient. Some limitations only became apparent through repeated use.


Experiment 2: Note Organizer
My second experiment was Note Organizer, an assistant designed to convert photographs of handwritten notes into structured digital documents.
The motivation was to reduce the effort involved in transcribing and reorganising handwritten material.
The configuration defined three main tasks:

Extract text from photographs of handwritten pages.
Organise and edit the extracted material into coherent sections.
Produce structured text, with Markdown or R Markdown available on request.

The assistant was also instructed to follow a sequential workflow: collect the photographs, ask for contextual information and wait until all pages had been uploaded before processing the notes.
An important part of the configuration concerned preserving the original information. The assistant was instructed not to introduce new concepts, to mark uncertain passages as [unclear] and to add explanatory examples only with explicit permission.
Observations and limitations
The assistant performed surprisingly well at recognising my handwriting. It also generally followed the intended page-by-page workflow.
However, preserving the original content proved more difficult. Despite explicit instructions not to invent information, the assistant occasionally introduced details that were not present in my notes.
The resulting documents also required several rounds of review and restructuring before I was satisfied with them.
Nevertheless, I found the assistant very useful. It substantially reduced the effort involved in creating an initial digital version of handwritten notes, even though the output still required careful editing.
This experiment highlighted the distinction between recognising information and faithfully interpreting it. Accurate transcription does not necessarily imply that the model will preserve the meaning of incomplete or ambiguous notes when reorganising them into coherent text.
It also demonstrated that instructions intended to prevent unsupported additions do not always work as expected.
